Challenges in Biological Engineering
To achieve the goals set for bioprocess engineering, advanced tools for strain engineering and
optimization will be required. These will include genetic engineering objectives such as the inte-gration of genes encoding high-activity and high-speci ﬁcity enzymes needed for product biosyn-
thesis, reprogramming of centr al carbon metabolism reactions [29], and also modulation of
cellular ﬂux partitioning and regulation in response to extracellular conditions. These modi ﬁcations
are summarized using the terms biological engineering and metabolic engineering, in other words
aiming at the best possible design of a production organism. We might coin a name for such or-
ganisms: 'fermenterphiles'. Recent technical and scienti ﬁc advances provide opportunities for ex-
citing novel research and development to improve biological engineering:
(i) Automated strain construction using novel genome-editing tools (e.g., CRISPR/Cas [30]),
leading to revolutionary acceleration of genet ic engineering and rapid strain development
[31,32] .
(ii) Improved strain robustness, both to rapid ﬂuctuations in the environment of large bioreactors
and to high concentrations of (toxic) products. Diverse host systems and extended genetic
resources (e.g., environmental screening [33,34] and new culture technologies [35]) will accel-
erate such developments.
(iii) Improved model-based predictions from increased understanding of microbial cells and con-
sortia thereof [36]. This includes the application of generic correlation models (such as arti ﬁcial
intelligence algorithms and machine learning) that can lead to fast work ﬂows to predict im-
proved strains.
(iv) Rapidly increasing ease and speed of identifying genes encoding new enzymes that catalyze
desired or interesting reactions. This includes whole-genome sequencing, annotation, docu-
mentation, and gene (function) discovery [37,38] .
Box 3. How Close Is Industry to 'Zero-Concepts'?
The Biosuccinium fermentation technology for succinic acid production serves as a leading example [66]. It uses acido-
philic conditions, well below the p Kaof the acid, which minimizes the addition of titrants during fermentation and product
recovery, resulting in close-to-zero associated waste salt production. However, owing to high proton shuttling across thecell membrane, the fermentation still requires oxygen as an electron acceptor to generate suf ﬁcient ATP via glucose dis-
similation to CO
2. Hence, zero-oxygen conditions are not yet feasible. However, metabolic engineering has minimized
the formation of organic byproducts and associated carbon spills, and cell retention further allows near-zero cell growth
conditions, with virtually no bleeds of spent biomass. O 2-enriched air can be used, which increases the CO 2concentration
in the process such that no additional CO 2supply is needed. Despite pH values around 3, and the use of minimal media,
aseptic conditions are still necessary to reduce contamination. Further, the total energy consumption remains signi ﬁcant
due to downstream water removal, despite the relatively high succinic acid titers ( N120 g/l). Summarizing, scale-up from
0.01 to N100 m3was successful, and signi ﬁcant strides were made regarding zero-factors, but further advances will be
necessary to achieve the zero-ideal. For other high-performance fermentation processes [7], such as for 1,3-propanediol
(that is still not anaerobic), farnesene (downstream processing is still necessary to separate the product from the broth),and gluconic acid (signi ﬁcant water still needs to be evaporated despite titers above 500 g/l), similar challenges remain
